overview: Spent nuclear fuel from power plants can be 'reprocessed' to recover material that can be used again as fuel. Today, facilities that reprocess spent fuel are classified as 'production facilities' under the Atomic Energy Act, the main U.S. nuclear law, which puts them in the strictest licensing category because traditional reprocessing separates out plutonium, a material usable in weapons. This bill removes that classification for reprocessing methods that do not separate plutonium from other similar heavy elements, so those facilities would be licensed under a different, less demanding category by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the federal agency that oversees nuclear safety. As of October 29, 2025, a Senate committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate's calendar, meaning it is eligible for a vote by the full Senate.
for: Supporters say newer recycling methods that keep plutonium mixed with other elements are harder to use for weapons, and updating the law would make it easier to reuse spent fuel and reduce nuclear waste.
against: Critics say any reprocessing still involves highly radioactive and potentially dangerous material, and easing the licensing category could reduce safety and security oversight.
